paras: The mob attack on a robbery victim at the American Tract Society Building was a street assault in downtown New York on Wednesday, 2 September 1903, in which a crowd beat a Black man who had just been robbed of his watch by two white men. Police clubbed the crowd apart, and the man left under police protection. The Boston Transcript's account, reprinted in Georgia and in the Black press, presented the attack as evidence of race prejudice in the North.

According to the Transcript, a "neatly dressed colored man" carrying a traveling bag was walking from a downtown office toward the Bridge when two white men passed him, one on each side. One tripped him while the other grabbed his watch and passed it to his companion, who escaped. The man got up and knocked the remaining robber down "in good manly fashion."

A crowd then gathered and, "without waiting to learn the merits of the situation," took the Black man for the aggressor and "pounced upon him with shouts of 'kill the nigger.'" He was receiving "very harsh usage" despite trying to explain when police interfered and broke up the mob "by a lively use of the club."

The man charged the robber he had knocked down, but because the watch was not found on him, the accused was allowed to go free. The victim, in the Transcript's words, "had to take himself off under police protection." No arrests among the crowd are reported, and no one involved is named.

Both surviving reports trace to the Boston Transcript, which drew the "moral" that, to a New York street crowd, a Black man had no right to defend himself against "white thugs." The Americus Times-Recorder in Georgia reprinted the item on 5 September under the headline "In New York, Also." It added that the Transcript doubtless thought this could not happen in Boston, "But some day worse things will occur there."
The St. Paul Appeal, a Black weekly, ran the same account on the same day without naming its source. It calls the man an "Afro-American" where the Transcript has "colored man" and "negro."

reader.title: Mob attack on a robbery victim at the American Tract Society Building
bases: A street crowd beat a Black man who had fought back against a robber, shouting "kill the nigger," until police broke it up; no one was killed (A2, A3).
Both surviving reports (A2, A3) reproduce one account, which A2 credits to the Boston Transcript; no New York local or independent report was found.

accounts.label: Boston Transcript account (reprinted)
accounts.gist: Two white men tripped and robbed a Black man of his watch; when he knocked one down, a crowd took him for the aggressor and attacked him shouting "kill the nigger" until police clubbed the mob apart, and the robber went free while the victim left under police protection.

framing.detail: Under 'In New York, Also,' the Americus Times-Recorder reprinted the Transcript's condemnation of the crowd but added that the Transcript 'doubtless' thought it could not happen in Boston, where 'worse things will occur' some day.
The St. Paul Appeal ran the same account without attribution, calling the man an 'Afro-American' and keeping its point that he had 'no right to protect himself against the attacks of white thugs.'

record_check.dossier: A white street crowd (unnamed) that collected after he knocked down one of two white robbers

record_check.dossier: Two white men tripped him and stole his watch before he knocked one down; police broke up the mob with clubs; the robber was let go because the watch was not found on him.
Both known white items (A1, A4) are the Graves address and not about this incident; the only white report found is the Americus Times-Recorder reprint of the Boston Transcript

info: Wednesday, the week before 5 September 1903 (2 September 1903)
In front of the American Tract Society Building, downtown New York, on the way toward the Bridge
One unnamed, "neatly dressed colored man" ("Afro-American" in the Appeal) carrying a traveling bag
None formal; the crowd "assumed that the black was the aggressor" after he knocked down a white man who had helped rob him
A street crowd that collected after he knocked down one of two white robbers; members not named
The victim left "under police protection"; the robber who took the watch escaped

sources.note: 'In New York, Also': full text of the Boston Transcript account, with a closing comment that 'worse things' will some day occur in Boston.

set_aside: John Temple Graves's Chicago address on 'The Problem of the Races'; refers only generally to a race riot in New York, not to this incident.
